title: Do two starts give the same primes for ninety?
description: Ninety is split into primes from two different starts, three times thirty and two times forty five. Each route is followed until only primes are left, and the two lists are compared. Keeko's doubt, that different starts give different answers, is tested against the lists.
teaching_notes: One idea: the primes at the end do not depend on the first split, only their order changes. Watch for students who expect a different factorisation from a different start.

source: Find the prime factorisation of 90 by starting with 3 × 30,
video_script.why: The child can split numbers but has not yet seen that the primes at the end do not depend on the first split.
video_script.substitution: Split each number until every piece is prime, then compare the primes from the two routes.
video_script.anchor: The number ninety with two starts, three times thirty and two times forty five, each leading to its own split tree.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the routes give two different answers because they start differently. Both routes end with one 2, two 3s and one 5, in a different order.
video_script.payoff_line: The primes are the same by either route.

final_answer.spoken: ninety is two times three times three times five, by either route

maths_rules: Both routes give one 2, two 3s and one 5: 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 = 90.
The book says the resulting prime factors are always the same, with perhaps a change in their order.
Slip: different starts do not give different primes.
video_script.design: One idea: the primes at the end do not depend on the first split. Assumes the child knows prime numbers. Wrong idea: different starts give different answers. The ninety stays on the board; two split trees sit side by side.
